questions.q: The type alias and the interface have different names. What does this print?
questions.explain: It compiles and runs. TypeScript compares shapes, not names: a has every property a User needs, so it fits. This is structural typing.

questions.q: What is the rule ZudoJS follows for interface and type?
questions.explain: Interfaces describe objects (and classes), can be extended with extends, and merge when two share a name. Unions, tuples and function types need a type alias.
options: Always use interface; it can describe anything
Use interface for object shapes, and type for everything else
Use interface for exported shapes and type for private ones

questions.q: Which of these can only be written with a type alias, not an interface?
questions.explain: An interface only describes object shapes. A union of literals, a tuple or a function type needs type, for example type Status = "todo" | "done".
options: A user with an id, an email and a name
An object with an optional property
An object with a readonly property

questions.q: With interface User { readonly id: number; email: string; name: string; nickname?: string }, which line does tsc accept?
questions.explain: nickname is optional, so it may be undefined. The others fail: id is read-only, email is a string (not null), and other is missing email.

questions.q: For nickname?: string, why does tsc reject user.nickname.toUpperCase()?
questions.explain: A user may have no nickname. Check first, or write user.nickname?.toUpperCase() or user.nickname ?? user.name.
options: Optional properties cannot be read, only written
The type is string | undefined, so user.nickname is possibly undefined
toUpperCase is not allowed on interface properties
The question mark makes the property a boolean

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The second user has no nickname, so reading it gives undefined, and ?? falls back to the full name.

questions.q: Which statement about readonly id: number is true?
questions.explain: Like every type, readonly is a compile-time promise. Plain JavaScript could still change the id. Use Object.freeze when the runtime must enforce it.
options: It freezes the object at runtime, like Object.freeze
It stops your TypeScript code from changing id, but it is removed before the code runs
It makes the id a secret that is not printed by console.log

questions.q: Plain JavaScript (an ES module, so strict mode is on). What does this print?
questions.explain: Object.freeze enforces read-only at runtime: in strict mode, assigning to a frozen property throws a TypeError, and the id stays 1. TypeScript's readonly does nothing at runtime.

questions.explain: readonly is shallow. It stops account.roles = [...], but the array itself can still change. Write readonly roles: readonly string[] to lock both.
options: TypeError: Cannot add property 1, object is not extensible

questions.explain: An Admin extends User, which extends Person, so every admin is also a person and greet accepts it. join(", ") puts a comma and a space between the permissions.

questions.q: What is type StoredUser = User & Timestamps?
questions.explain: & is an intersection: it combines shapes. | (a union) would be "one or the other".
options: A value that is either a User or a Timestamps
A value that has all the properties of both User and Timestamps
Only the properties that User and Timestamps have in common
A list with one user and one timestamp

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An intersection needs every property from both shapes. At runtime it is just one plain object with four keys.

questions.q: greet only reads person.name. Which parameter type is best?
questions.explain: A function should ask for the smallest shape it needs. Then admins, users and stored users are all accepted, because they all have a name.
options: person: Person, the smallest shape that has a name
person: any, so anything can be passed

questions.q: With type Role = "member" | "editor" | "admin", which line does tsc reject?
questions.explain: A union of literal types allows only the listed words. "superuser" is not one of them, so the error is Type '"superuser"' is not assignable to type 'Role'.

questions.q: Which line does tsc reject?
questions.explain: A let can change later, so status gets the wide type string, which is not assignable to the union. A const never changes, so fixedStatus keeps the literal type "active".
questions.code:
let status = "active";                                        // line 1
const fixedStatus = "active";                                 // line 2
const allowed: "active" | "suspended" = status;               // line 3
const alsoAllowed: "active" | "suspended" = fixedStatus;      // line 4

questions.q: You want a let variable that may only ever hold "active" or "suspended". How do you write it?
questions.explain: Annotate the variable with the union. Without the annotation, a let is widened to string and any text would be allowed.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Literal types exist only for the compiler. At runtime role and fixedStatus are ordinary strings, and typeof says so.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Checking event.kind === "logout" narrows the event, so event.minutes is allowed and is a number. Login events have no minutes and are skipped: 30 + 15 is 45.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The object has no email property, so the in check is false and the last line runs. A plain string is caught by the typeof check first.

questions.q: In describeContact, why is contact.country allowed on the last line without any check?
questions.explain: TypeScript follows each check and narrows the union. Every branch that returned removes a member, so at the end only { phone: string; country: string } remains.
options: Because country exists on every member of the union
After the typeof and "email" in contact checks return, only the phone shape is left
Because in converts the contact to a phone
TypeScript does not check the last line of a function

questions.q: What makes a union a discriminated union?
questions.explain: The shared property (often kind or status) tells the shapes apart. Checking it in a switch or if narrows the value to one shape.
options: All members have exactly the same properties
Every member shares one property, like kind, with a different literal value in each
It is written with & instead of |
Its members are classes, not objects

questions.explain: The switch on state.kind picks the right case, and in each case TypeScript knows exactly which properties that state has.
options:

invited by user 1

invited by user undefined

active, last login undefined

questions.q: Inside case "active": of that switch, what happens if you read state.reason?
questions.explain: In that case, state is narrowed to { kind: "active"; lastLogin: string }. Only kind and lastLogin exist there.
options: tsc reports an error: an active state has no reason
It gives the reason of the last suspended user
It is allowed, because reason is in the union

questions.q: Why is a discriminated union better than one shape with many optional properties, like { kind: string; lastLogin?: string; reason?: string; until?: string }?
questions.explain: With many optional properties, nonsense combinations compile and every read needs a check. With a discriminated union, each state carries exactly its own data.
options: It uses less memory at runtime
Impossible states, like an active user with a suspension reason, cannot even be written
Optional properties are not allowed in interfaces
It avoids the need for a switch

questions.q: You add { kind: "deleted"; deletedAt: string } to AccountState. The switch has the const unreachable: never = state; default but no "deleted" case. What happens?
questions.explain: This is the exhaustiveness check. The new state reaches default, where only never is allowed, so every switch that forgot it stops compiling.
options: tsc reports that the deleted state is not assignable to never, at that switch
The code throws when a deleted user logs in, but compiles

questions.q: In the user module, NewUser (what someone sends to sign up) has only email and name. Why no id, role or state?
questions.explain: If the client could send a role, anyone could sign up as an admin. The server gives every new user its own id, the role "member" and an active state.
options: They are optional, so they are left out to save space
The server decides those, never the client
Interfaces cannot have more than two properties
They are added by TypeScript automatically

questions.q: This insecure update compiles without errors. What does it print?
questions.explain: JSON.parse returns any, so the compiler trusts it, and the spread copies every property the client sent, including role. Eve made herself an admin. This hole is called mass assignment; copy allowed fields by name instead.
options: TypeError: role is not in ProfileUpdate

questions.q: How should updateProfile apply a profile change that came from a request body?
questions.explain: Types describe what you expect; they do not remove what an attacker adds. The spread and Object.assign copy every property the client sent. Reversing the spread order still copies properties the user does not have yet, so copy allowed fields by name.
options: Copy only the fields a user may change, by name: if (changes.name !== undefined) user.name = changes.name;
Spread the changes first, then the user: { ...changes, ...user }

questions.q: The same attack, against the safe version. What does this print?
questions.explain: Only name and email are copied, by name. email was not sent, so it is left alone, and the extra role in the request is simply ignored.

questions.q: Finish area for this discriminated union, with a switch on shape.kind: a square's area is size * size, a rectangle's is width * height. The program should print 9 12.
questions.explain: In each case, shape is narrowed to one member, so only its own properties are allowed. Every case returns, so the compiler knows the function cannot reach its end.

questions.q: A "deleted" state was added to the union, and the exhaustiveness check now fails. Add the missing case so the program compiles and prints deleted on 2026-09-01.
questions.explain: Add case "deleted": returning `deleted on ${state.deletedAt}`. Then nothing reaches default and state is never there again. Without the fix, the browser runs the code anyway and prints the whole object, because it does not check types.

questions.explain: Copying fields by name ignores anything extra the client sends. Object.assign(user, changes) or a spread would copy role too, even though the types say it is not there: that is mass assignment.

questions.q: Write interface Admin that extends User and adds a readonly permissions list of strings. Then finish canWrite: true when the admin has the users:write permission. The program should print true false.
questions.explain: interface Admin extends User { readonly permissions: readonly string[] } copies in id and name and adds the list. includes only reads, so it works on a readonly array.

questions.q: Finish canChangeRoles: only an admin whose account is active may change roles. Deny everyone else. The program should print true false false.
questions.explain: Return true only when every rule says yes. Checking only the role would let a suspended admin like Bob keep changing roles.

questions.q: Finish withTimestamps: return a new object with all the user's properties plus createdAt and updatedAt, both set to now. The return type is the intersection User & Timestamps. The program should print Ada 2026-09-23 2026-09-23.
questions.explain: An intersection needs every property from both shapes. Spreading the user and adding the two timestamps builds exactly that. Here the spread is safe: the user object is your own data, not a request body.
